notes.front: What is GitHub Packages?
notes.back: GitHub’s package hosting service: you host software packages privately or publicly and use them as dependencies in your projects.
notes.explanation: Packages hosted there can be private or public, and your projects consume them as dependencies.
notes.example: Like publishing a library to the public npm registry, but the package lives on GitHub next to its repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”
notes.evidence: is a software package hosting service that allows you to host your software packages privately or publicly and use packages as dependencies in your projects.

notes.front: What is Azure Artifacts?
notes.back: The Azure DevOps service for managing all your dependencies from a single feed, where packages are stored, managed and shared.
notes.explanation: The feeds can share packages within a team, across organisations or, for existing public projects, publicly online.
notes.example: Like a private copy of nuget.org and npmjs.com run by your Azure DevOps organisation, holding your own packages too.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Artifacts?”, “What is Azure Artifacts?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts provides developers with a streamlined way to manage all their dependencies from a single feed. These feeds serve as repositories for storing, managing, and sharing packages within your team, across organizations, or, for existing public projects, publicly online.

notes.front: In Azure Artifacts, what is a feed?
notes.back: An organisational construct for storing, managing and sharing packages while controlling who can access them.
notes.explanation: One feed is not limited to one package type: it can hold npm, NuGet, Maven, Python, Cargo and Universal Packages together.
notes.example: Like a shared team drive for packages, with its own permissions, holding both npm and NuGet packages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure Artifacts feeds?”, “What are Azure Artifacts feeds?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts feeds are organizational constructs that allow you to store, manage, and share your packages while controlling access. A single feed can host multiple package types, including npm, NuGet, Maven, Python, Cargo, and Universal Packages packages.

notes.front: What is a public feed in Azure Artifacts?
notes.back: A feed whose packages anyone on the internet can use, without being a member of your organisation or signing in.
notes.explanation: Users need neither membership of your organisation nor a sign-in to the Azure DevOps portal.
notes.example: Like a public GitHub repository’s releases page, but serving installable packages from an Azure DevOps project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure Artifacts feeds?”, “Public feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Public feeds allow you to share your packages publicly with anyone on the internet. Users do not need to be members of your organization, or sign in to the Azure DevOps portal to access packages in a public feed.

notes.front: What is a feed view?
notes.back: A way to share a chosen subset of a feed’s package versions with consumers.
notes.explanation: It lets you offer tested and validated versions while holding back those still in development or below your quality standards.
notes.example: Like a shop window showing only finished stock, while the workshop behind it (the whole feed) holds work in progress.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “What are feed views?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Feed views allow developers to share a specific subset of package versions with consumers. This is useful when you want to provide access to packages that have been tested and validated, while withholding those still under development or that don’t meet your quality standards.

notes.front: What is an upstream source in Azure Artifacts?
notes.back: A source, such as a public registry or another feed, whose packages your feed can serve; packages installed from it are saved to your feed.
notes.explanation: It lets one feed hold both the packages you publish and those installed from registries such as nuget.org or npmjs.com.
notes.example: Like a library that orders books from other libraries on request and then keeps a copy on its own shelves.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “What are upstream sources?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts upstream sources allow developers to store packages from various origins in a single feed, including packages published to the feed and those installed from public registries like *NuGet.org* or *npmjs.com*. Once upstream sources are enabled, any package installed from an upstream source is automatically saved to your feed.

notes.front: What is Semantic Versioning (SemVer)?
notes.back: A version scheme of major.minor.patch in which the number that changes tells users what kind of change was made to the public interface.
notes.explanation: Version numbers and the way they change carry meaning about the code and what was modified from one version to the next.
notes.example: Like a label on a jar saying “same recipe, new lid” or “new recipe”: moving from 2.3.1 to 2.3.2 signals only a fix.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Introduction”
notes.evidence: Consider a version format of X.Y.Z (Major.Minor.Patch). Bug fixes not affecting the API increment the patch version, backward compatible API additions/changes increment the minor version, and backward incompatible API changes increment the major version. We call this system “Semantic Versioning.” Under this scheme, version numbers and the way they change convey meaning about the underlying code

notes.front: What is Calendar Versioning (CalVer)?
notes.back: A versioning convention based on the project’s release calendar, usually using part of the release date, instead of arbitrary numbers.
notes.explanation: The date-based pattern emerged as a common practice and came to be called Calendar Versioning.
notes.example: Like a magazine numbered by issue date, such as a release called 26.09 for September 2026.
notes.source: calver.org, “Calendar Versioning”, “Calendar Versioning”
notes.evidence: Another common versioning pattern incorporates a time-based element, usually part of the release date. This date-based approach has come to be called Calendar Versioning, or CalVer for short.

notes.front: In Azure Pipelines, what is a pipeline artifact?
notes.back: Files a pipeline run publishes so that later stages, or another pipeline, can download them.
notes.explanation: Azure Pipelines lets you download artifacts from earlier stages or from another pipeline, and publish an artifact as a pipeline artifact.
notes.example: Like a sealed parcel the build stage posts and the deploy stage collects, instead of each stage rebuilding the web app.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Using Azure Pipelines, you can download artifacts from earlier stages in your pipeline or from another pipeline. You can also publish your artifact to a file share or make it available as a pipeline artifact.

notes.front: What is a `.artifactignore` file?
notes.back: A file, written in a syntax like `.gitignore`, that lists the files to leave out when publishing artifacts.
notes.explanation: It must sit in the directory given by the `targetPath` argument of the Publish Pipeline Artifacts task.
notes.example: Like a `.gitignore`, but it filters what goes into a pipeline artifact, not what goes into a commit.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Use .artifactignore” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: `.artifactignore` uses a similar syntax to `.gitignore` (with few limitations) to specify which files should be ignored when publishing artifacts. Make sure that the *.artifactignore* file is located within the directory specified by the *targetPath* argument of your Publish Pipeline Artifacts task.

notes.front: In Azure Pipelines, what is the run number format?
notes.back: The pattern that names each run, built from text, special tokens and variables, which you can customise.
notes.explanation: A unique run number identifies each run; with no format set, each run simply gets a unique integer.
notes.example: Like numbering invoices as “2026-09-0042” instead of plain “42”, so the name says when it was made.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run and build numbers” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you don't specify a build name in YAML pipelines, or you leave the **Name** or **Build number format** field blank in Classic pipelines, each run gets a unique integer as its name. Build names can use other characters, tokens, and variables. You can customize run and build numbers by using naming patterns, special tokens, and predefined or user-defined variables.

notes.front: What is a build tag in Azure DevOps?
notes.back: A label you add to a build to categorise it, so you can filter for and find particular builds.
notes.explanation: The tags then act as filters when you look for particular builds.
notes.example: Like a sticky note saying “shipped” on a folder in a filing cabinet, but applied to a pipeline run.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add, remove, and use build tags”, “Add, remove, and use build tags” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Build tags in Azure DevOps help you categorize and organize your builds, making it easier to filter and locate specific builds.

notes.front: In GitHub Actions, what is a workflow artifact?
notes.back: A file or collection of files produced during a workflow run, kept after the job ends and shareable with other jobs in that workflow.
notes.explanation: Artifacts let data outlive the job that made it, for example build and test output after the run has ended.
notes.example: Like a pipeline artifact in Azure Pipelines, but uploaded and downloaded by GitHub Actions workflow steps.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow artifacts”, “About workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: An artifact is a file or collection of files produced during a workflow run. Artifacts allow you to persist data after a job has completed, and share that data with another job in the same workflow.

notes.front: What is an artifact attestation?
notes.back: A cryptographically signed claim about how and where your software was built, which consumers can verify.
notes.explanation: It gives unfalsifiable provenance and integrity guarantees for the software you build.
notes.example: Like a signed certificate of origin shipped with goods, stating which factory and production line made them.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About artifact attestations” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-artifact-attestations.md)
notes.evidence: Artifact attestations enable you to create unfalsifiable provenance and integrity guarantees for the software you build. In turn, people who consume your software can verify where and how your software was built.

notes.front: What does GitHub Packages give you by keeping your source code and packages in one place?
notes.back: Integrated permissions management and billing, so software development is centralised on GitHub.
notes.explanation: Code and packages share one home, so access and billing are managed together.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “About GitHub Packages”
notes.evidence: combines your source code and packages in one place to provide integrated permissions management{% ifversion fpt or ghec %} and billing{% endif %}, so you can centralize your software development on

notes.front: In GitHub Packages, a JavaScript package is described by {{c1::`package.json`}} and published with the `npm` client.
notes.back: `package.json`
notes.explanation: The npm registry uses the Node package manager’s own format and client.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “Support for package registries”
notes.evidence: | JavaScript | Node package manager | `package.json`  | `npm` |

notes.front: In GitHub Packages, `.NET` packages use the {{c1::NuGet}} registry, with the `nupkg` format and the `dotnet` command-line client.
notes.back: NuGet
notes.explanation: The registry follows `.NET`’s own package manager.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “Support for package registries”
notes.evidence: | .NET | NuGet package management for .NET | `nupkg`  |  `dotnet` CLI |

notes.front: A Java team builds with a `build.gradle.kts` file and wants to publish its library to GitHub Packages. Which client does it use?
notes.choices:
A) `mvn`
B) `gradle`
C) `npm`
D) `dotnet`
notes.back: B) `gradle`
notes.choicesExplained: A is the client for Maven projects described by `pom.xml`. C is for JavaScript packages. D is for `.NET` packages.
notes.explanation: The Gradle registry takes `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts` files and the `gradle` client.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “Support for package registries”
notes.evidence: | Java | Gradle build automation tool for Java | `build.gradle` or `build.gradle.kts`  | `gradle`  |

notes.front: Where do the permissions for a package in GitHub Packages come from?
notes.back: Either inherited from the repository that hosts the package, or defined for specific users or organisations.
notes.explanation: Some registries support only permissions inherited from a repository.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “Overview of package permissions”
notes.evidence: The permissions for a package are either inherited from the repository where the package is hosted, or can be defined for specific users or organizations. Some registries only support permissions inherited from a repository.

notes.front: A team keeps all its code on GitHub and wants its container images hosted beside that code, with access and billing handled in the same place. What should it use?
notes.choices:
A) A public feed in Azure Artifacts
B) A pipeline artifact
C) A Git tag on each release
D) GitHub Packages
notes.back: D) GitHub Packages
notes.choicesExplained: A lives in an Azure DevOps project, not beside the GitHub code. B stores a pipeline run’s files, not a package registry. C marks a commit; it hosts no images.
notes.explanation: GitHub Packages hosts packages, including containers, beside the source code with integrated permissions and billing.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Introduction to GitHub Packages”, “About GitHub Packages”
notes.evidence: combines your source code and packages in one place to provide integrated permissions management{% ifversion fpt or ghec %} and billing{% endif %}

notes.front: What are two package types that Azure Artifacts supports?
notes.back: Any two of: NuGet, npm, Python, Maven, Cargo and Universal Packages.
notes.explanation: Universal Packages sit beside the language-specific package types in that list.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Artifacts?”, “What is Azure Artifacts?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts supports multiple package types, including NuGet, npm, Python, Maven, Cargo, and Universal Packages.

notes.front: How much free Azure Artifacts storage does each organisation get?
notes.back: 2 GiB.
notes.explanation: The free tier is meant for evaluating Azure Artifacts; you can raise the storage limit as usage grows.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Artifacts?”, “What is Azure Artifacts?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts provides 2 GiB of free storage for each organization. This free tier is designed to help you evaluate if Azure Artifacts fits your workflow. As your organization begins handling more critical tasks, increase artifacts storage limit to ensure you have the appropriate resources.

notes.front: A team has a `.NET` service and an npm front end and wants all their dependencies managed from one place in Azure DevOps. What is the simplest set-up?
notes.choices:
A) One feed for each package type
B) Two separate organisations
C) A pipeline artifact for each package
D) A single Azure Artifacts feed holding both the NuGet and npm packages
notes.back: D) A single Azure Artifacts feed holding both the NuGet and npm packages
notes.choicesExplained: A is not needed: one feed can host several package types. C passes files between pipeline stages; it is not a package feed. B splits the team for no reason.
notes.explanation: A feed is not limited to a single package type.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Artifacts key concepts”, “Feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: A feed isn't limited to a single package type and can host various package types such as npm, NuGet, Maven, Python, Cargo, and Universal Packages.

notes.front: A company needs one private package service for Python wheels, Cargo crates and Universal Packages. Going by each service’s documented formats, which fits?
notes.choices:
A) GitHub Packages
B) A Git tag
C) Azure Artifacts
D) A workflow artifact
notes.back: C) Azure Artifacts
notes.choicesExplained: A lists npm, RubyGems, Maven, Gradle, NuGet and Docker, not Python, Cargo or Universal Packages. B names a commit, not a package store. D keeps a run’s files; it is not a registry.
notes.explanation: Azure Artifacts lists Python, Cargo and Universal Packages among its package types.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What is Azure Artifacts?”, “What is Azure Artifacts?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts supports multiple package types, including NuGet, npm, Python, Maven, Cargo, and Universal Packages.

notes.front: Which scope does Azure Artifacts recommend for new feeds: project or organisation?
notes.back: Project.
notes.explanation: You choose the scope when creating the feed, and the documentation recommends scoping new feeds to a project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Project-scoped vs organization-scoped feeds”, “Feed scopes: Project vs organization feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When creating a new feed in Azure Artifacts, you can choose to scope it to either a project or your organization, depending on your scenario. However, Azure Artifacts recommends scoping new feeds to a project.

notes.front: How does the visibility of a project-scoped feed differ from that of an organisation-scoped feed?
notes.back: A project-scoped feed inherits the project’s visibility; an organisation-scoped feed is always private by default.
notes.explanation: Only a project-scoped feed can pick up a public project’s visibility.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Project-scoped vs organization-scoped feeds”, “Project-scoped vs organization-scoped feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | **Visibility**    | Inherits the visibility of the project.                                                                       | Always private by default.                                                        |

notes.front: Can an organisation-scoped feed be converted into a project-scoped feed?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: Organisation-scoped feeds are viewable from any project in the organisation, and they stay organisation-scoped.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure Artifacts feeds?”, “Feed types” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Feeds scoped to an organization. They’re viewable from any project within the organization. Organization-scoped feeds **cannot** be converted into project-scoped feeds.

notes.front: A pipeline in project Beta must download packages from a project-scoped feed in project Alpha. What access does Beta’s project build service need?
notes.choices:
A) Only the Feed Owner role
B) Membership of Alpha’s Readers group and a feed role such as Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)
C) Nothing: project-scoped feeds are visible to every project
D) Only membership of Beta’s Contributors group
notes.back: B) Membership of Alpha’s Readers group and a feed role such as Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)
notes.choicesExplained: A grants far more than reading, and still leaves out project-level access. C is wrong: a project-scoped feed is viewable only within its hosting project. D is permission in the wrong project.
notes.explanation: Access must be granted both at the hosting project level and at the feed level.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Project-scoped vs organization-scoped feeds”, “How can I access a project-scoped feed in another project from my pipeline?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To allow a pipeline to access a project-scoped feed in a different project, you need to grant access both at the project level (where the feed is hosted) and the feed level.

notes.front: Where can you create a public feed in Azure Artifacts?
notes.back: Only within an existing public project, as a project-scoped feed.
notes.explanation: Public feeds inherit the visibility settings of the hosting project.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are Azure Artifacts feeds?”, “Public feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Public feeds are **project-scoped** and inherit the visibility settings of the hosting project. Here are some important key points: - You can only create public feeds within existing public projects.

notes.front: What happens to public feeds when Azure DevOps converts existing public projects to private, starting in 2027?
notes.back: They are no longer publicly accessible.
notes.explanation: A public feed takes its visibility from its hosting project, so it follows the project to private.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Project-scoped vs organization-scoped feeds”, “Feed scopes: Project vs organization feeds” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Starting in 2027, existing public projects will automatically convert to private. When that happens, public feeds will no longer be publicly accessible because they inherit the visibility of the hosting project.

notes.front: How long do deleted packages stay in the Azure Artifacts Recycle Bin, and who can restore them?
notes.back: 30 days; only a feed owner can restore them.
notes.explanation: After 30 days Azure Artifacts deletes them permanently.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Artifacts key concepts”, “Retention and the Recycle Bin” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Deleted packages are placed in the Recycle Bin and remain there for 30 days before Azure Artifacts permanently deletes them. Only a feed owner can restore packages from the Recycle Bin.

notes.front: Once a package version is published to an Azure Artifacts feed, that version number is {{c1::permanently reserved}}.
notes.back: permanently reserved
notes.explanation: You cannot upload a newer revision under the same number, nor delete it and republish with that number.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Artifacts key concepts”, “Immutability” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: After you publish a specific version of a package to a feed, that version number is permanently reserved. You can't upload a newer revision of the package under the same version number, and you can't delete it and republish a new package with that same version number.

notes.front: A job publishes version 3.1.0 of a package to a feed, then a later job fails. When the team reruns the failed jobs, the publish step fails with “package already exists”. What does the documentation suggest?
notes.choices:
A) Use conditions so a job runs only if the previous job succeeded
B) Overwrite 3.1.0 with a new upload
C) Promote 3.1.0 to the @release view
D) Delete 3.1.0 from the feed and republish it
notes.back: A) Use conditions so a job runs only if the previous job succeeded
notes.choicesExplained: D and B are impossible: a published version number is permanently reserved. C changes who sees the package; it does not let you publish again.
notes.explanation: Packages are immutable, so rerunning a job that already published fails; conditions avoid the rerun error.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Publish artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Rerunning failed jobs will fail if the package has been published. A good way to approach this if you want to be able to rerun failed jobs without facing an error *package already exists*, is to use Conditions to only run if the previous job succeeded.

notes.front: What can a user connected to a feed view use?
notes.back: Only packages published to that view and packages previously saved from upstream sources: views are read-only.
notes.explanation: Packages are published only to the base feed; a view exposes what was promoted into it.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Default view” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Feed views are **read-only**, which means that users connected to a view can only use packages that are published to that view and/or packages previously saved from upstream sources.

notes.front: SemVer tells consumers the nature and risk of a change. What do feed views communicate instead?
notes.back: The quality of the change: whether a package passed validation.
notes.explanation: Quality is known only after validation, so it cannot go in the numeric part of the version.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Quality of the change” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The **quality** of the change isn't generally known until the validation process is complete. This is determined after validation, once the package is built and tested. Because of this, it's not feasible to communicate the quality of the change in the numerical segment of the version number

notes.front: Auditors find that a contractor with no feed permissions still downloaded packages through the @release view. What must you change?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: views cannot grant downloads
B) Delete the @local view
C) Restrict access to both the feed and the view, for example setting the view to Specific people
D) Convert the feed to organisation scope
notes.back: C) Restrict access to both the feed and the view, for example setting the view to Specific people
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: view access alone allows downloads. B would remove the view holding every published package and still leave `@release` open. D would make the feed private by default but does not narrow who can use the view.
notes.explanation: Full restriction needs limits on both the feed and its views.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed views settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To restrict access to the view, change **Visibility** to **Specific people**.

notes.front: Which default feed view contains every package published to the feed and every package saved from upstream sources?
notes.back: `@local`, the default view.
notes.explanation: The other two default views, `@prerelease` and `@release`, are the ones you may rename or delete.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Azure Artifacts key concepts”, “Feed views” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: `@local` is the default view and contains every package published directly to the feed as well as every package saved from upstream sources.

notes.front: Which two default feed views are only suggestions that you can rename or delete?
notes.back: `@prerelease` and `@release`.
notes.explanation: Every feed starts with three views; `@local` is the one that stays as the default.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Default view” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Every Artifacts feed includes three views by default: `@local`, `@prerelease`, and `@release`. The latter two are suggested views that you can rename or delete as needed.

notes.front: Consumers of a shared library should see only versions that have passed validation and met the team’s quality bar. Which view should they connect to?
notes.choices:
A) `@release`
B) `@local`
C) `@prerelease`
D) The base feed with no view
notes.back: A) `@release`
notes.choicesExplained: B and D include every published version, validated or not. C is the suggested view for versions not yet released.
notes.explanation: The `@Release` view is the one the documentation uses to share only validated packages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Quality of the change” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Using the `@Release` view, you can share only packages that have passed validation and met your quality bar.

notes.front: Which feed roles can promote a package to a view?
notes.back: Feed Publisher (Contributor) or Feed Owner.
notes.explanation: Promotion is one of the rights that begins at the publisher role.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Promote packages and manage feed views”, “Promote a package to a view” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: You must be a **Feed Publisher (Contributor)** or a **Feed Owner** to promote packages to a view.

notes.front: A release manager promoted an untested package version to `@release` by mistake. What can she do about the promotion itself?
notes.choices:
A) Nothing: promotion cannot be reverted, so she must deal with it another way
B) Demote it back to `@prerelease`
C) Republish the same version number without the view
D) Ask a Feed Reader to remove the view
notes.back: A) Nothing: promotion cannot be reverted, so she must deal with it another way
notes.choicesExplained: B is not supported. C is impossible: the version number is permanently reserved. D gives a role that cannot even promote.
notes.explanation: Azure Artifacts does not support demotion, so promote only validated versions.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Promote packages and manage feed views”, “Promote a package to a view” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts doesn't support package demotion. Once a package is promoted, it can't be reverted to a previous view.

notes.front: What visibility must your feed have before other Azure Artifacts feeds can use it as an upstream source?
notes.back: Members of your organisation, or members of your Microsoft Entra ID, depending on your scenario.
notes.explanation: The visibility is set on the feed that other feeds will use as their upstream.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Feed views and upstream sources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To allow other Azure Artifacts feeds to use your feed as an upstream source, you must set your feed's visibility to **members of your organization**, or **members of your Microsoft Entra ID**, depending on your scenario.

notes.front: Which benefit of upstream sources comes from your feed keeping metadata about the packages it saved?
notes.back: Package integrity: you can verify you are using the original versions, not copies or malicious versions.
notes.explanation: Retained metadata lets you check the authenticity of saved packages.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Why use upstream sources?” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Package Integrity**: Your feed retains metadata about packages saved from upstream sources, allowing you to verify their authenticity and ensure you're using the original versions, not copies or potentially malicious versions.

notes.front: npmjs.com is unreachable for two hours. A team whose feed has npmjs.com as an upstream source rebuilds an app whose packages were installed through the feed last week. What happens?
notes.choices:
A) The build restores the packages from the feed, which saved copies of them
B) The build waits until npmjs.com returns
C) The build must switch to a pipeline artifact
D) The build fails: every package is fetched from npmjs.com each time
notes.back: A) The build restores the packages from the feed, which saved copies of them
notes.choicesExplained: D and B ignore the saved copies. C is unrelated: pipeline artifacts pass a run’s files between stages.
notes.explanation: Packages installed from an upstream source are saved to the feed, so they remain available during the outage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Save packages from upstream sources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the public registry experiences downtime, maintenance, or becomes temporarily unavailable, you can still retrieve the necessary packages from your feed and continue your development.

notes.front: For a deterministic restore, how many feeds should your `nuget.config` or `.npmrc` reference?
notes.back: Only one: the feed with upstream sources enabled.
notes.explanation: The feed can then provide a deterministic restore through its upstream sources.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Use a single feed in your configuration file” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In order for your feed to provide a deterministic restore, make sure that your configuration file (such as *nuget.config* or *npmrc*) references **only one feed** with upstream sources enabled.

notes.front: A `nuget.config` lists both the team’s Azure Artifacts feed (with nuget.org as an upstream source) and nuget.org itself. Restores sometimes pick different versions. What fixes this?
notes.choices:
A) Add a second upstream source
B) Reference only the Azure Artifacts feed in the configuration file
C) Promote every package to `@release`
D) Switch the feed to organisation scope
notes.back: B) Reference only the Azure Artifacts feed in the configuration file
notes.choicesExplained: A adds sources instead of removing the second one. C changes visibility, not how the client picks sources. D changes scope, not restore order.
notes.explanation: NuGet queries all configured feeds in parallel; one feed with upstreams gives a fixed search order.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Search order” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: NuGet sends parallel queries to all the feeds in the configuration file and processes responses in a first-in, first-out (FIFO) manner, which can lead to inconsistent results.

notes.front: An Azure Artifacts feed searches first packages published directly to it, then {{c1::packages already saved from an upstream source}}, then the upstream sources in their configured order.
notes.back: packages already saved from an upstream source
notes.explanation: Each upstream source is searched in the order it is listed in the feed’s configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Search order” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: 1. Packages that have been published directly to the feed. 1. Packages that have been saved from an upstream source. 1. Packages available from upstream sources. Each upstream source is searched in the order it's listed in the feed's configuration.

notes.front: When a feed mixes other feeds and public registries as upstream sources, where does Microsoft recommend placing the public registries?
notes.back: First in the list of upstream sources.
notes.explanation: With several kinds of source, each upstream is searched in the order set in the feed’s configuration.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Order your upstream sources intentionally” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: However, when managing multiple sources, such as a combination of feeds and public registries, each upstream source is searched in the order defined in the feed’s configuration settings. In these cases, we recommend placing the public registries first in the list of upstream sources.

notes.front: Your security team rebuilds a patched copy of an open-source logging library and keeps it in an internal feed. Where should that feed sit among your upstream sources?
notes.choices:
A) Before the other public registries
B) It should not be an upstream source
C) Last, after all public registries
D) Order does not matter
notes.back: A) Before the other public registries
notes.choicesExplained: C would let the public version win. B loses the patched copy entirely. D is true only when the upstreams are all public registries.
notes.explanation: Placing the customised packages first ensures they are used instead of the public ones.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Order your upstream sources intentionally” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your organization follows this practice, place the upstream source containing these customized OSS packages before other public registries. This ensures your customized versions are used instead of the public ones.

notes.front: Whose package installs from an upstream source are automatically saved to the feed?
notes.back: Installs by a collaborator or higher.
notes.explanation: The copy is saved automatically once the upstream source is enabled on the feed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are upstream sources?”, “Save packages from upstream sources” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When an upstream source is enabled on your feed, Azure Artifacts automatically saves a copy of any package installed by a collaborator or higher from that upstream source.

notes.front: A developer with the Feed Reader role installs a new package through the feed from its nuget.org upstream, but it is not saved to the feed. What is the least role that would make installs save packages?
notes.choices:
A) Feed Owner
B) Feed Publisher (Contributor)
C) Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)
D) Project Collection Administrator
notes.back: C) Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)
notes.choicesExplained: B and A can also save, but they grant more than needed. D is an organisation-wide administrator role, far beyond what is needed.
notes.explanation: Saving packages from upstream sources starts at the Collaborator role.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)**: Can save packages from upstream sources, in addition to all **Reader** permissions.

notes.front: Is the Allow External Versions setting for a package on or off by default, and what does that protect against?
notes.back: Off, which reduces exposure to potentially malicious packages from public registries.
notes.explanation: Only when it is switched on do public versions of that package become available to save to the feed.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Safeguard against malicious public packages”, “Allow externally sourced versions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, this option is disabled, adding an extra layer of security by reducing exposure to potentially malicious packages from public registries.

notes.front: A feed owner turns Allow External Versions off for a package after several public versions were already saved to the feed. What happens to those saved versions?
notes.choices:
A) They are deleted
B) They move to the Recycle Bin
C) They remain accessible
D) They are demoted to `@prerelease`
notes.back: C) They remain accessible
notes.choicesExplained: A and B are wrong: changing the setting does not remove saved versions. D is wrong: Azure Artifacts has no demotion.
notes.explanation: The setting governs new versions from public registries, not versions already saved.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Safeguard against malicious public packages”, “Allow externally sourced versions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Changing this setting does not affect package versions already saved to the feed. Those versions remain accessible regardless of this setting.

notes.front: Which feed role can list, view and download packages, but nothing more?
notes.back: Feed Reader.
notes.explanation: It is the lowest of the four feed roles.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Feed Reader**: Can list, view, and download packages from the feed.

notes.front: Which feed role adds the rights to publish, promote, deprecate and unlist packages?
notes.back: Feed Publisher (Contributor).
notes.explanation: It has all Collaborator permissions as well.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Feed Publisher (Contributor)**: Can publish, promote, deprecate, and unlist packages, in addition to all **Collaborator** permissions.

notes.front: Which feed role alone can manage upstream sources, allow external package versions and delete packages or the feed?
notes.back: Feed Owner.
notes.explanation: It also manages feed settings and has every Contributor permission.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: **Feed Owner**: Can manage feed settings, manage upstream sources, allow external package versions, and delete packages or the feed itself, in addition to all **Contributor** permissions.

notes.front: Which feed role do the Project Collection Build Service and the project-level Build Service get by default?
notes.back: Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator).
notes.explanation: That role reads packages and saves from upstreams, but cannot publish.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Feed settings” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: By default, the *Project Collection Build Service* (organization-scoped) and the project-level *Build Service* (project-scoped) are assigned the **Feed and Upstream Reader (Collaborator)** role.

notes.front: A pipeline restores packages from a feed without trouble, but its new step that publishes a package to the same feed is refused. What should you change?
notes.choices:
A) Give the build identities the Feed Reader role
B) Add an upstream source
C) Enable Allow External Versions
D) Give the Project Collection Build Service and the project-level Build Service the Feed Publisher (Contributor) role
notes.back: D) Give the Project Collection Build Service and the project-level Build Service the Feed Publisher (Contributor) role
notes.choicesExplained: A is lower than the Collaborator role they already have. C concerns public versions, not publishing. B adds sources to read from, not the right to publish.
notes.explanation: The build identities start as Collaborators; publishing needs the Contributor role on both identities.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Manage permissions”, “Pipelines permissions” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If the pipeline needs to publish packages, assign the **Feed Publisher (Contributor)** role to both the *Project Collection Build Service* identity and the project-level *Build Service* identity.

notes.front: Under SemVer, which part of the version do you increment when you make backward compatible bug fixes?
notes.back: The patch version.
notes.explanation: A bug fix is an internal change that fixes incorrect behaviour.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Patch version Z (x.y.Z | x > 0) MUST be incremented if only backward compatible bug fixes are introduced. A bug fix is defined as an internal change that fixes incorrect behavior.

notes.front: Under SemVer, which part of the version do you increment when you add functionality in a backward compatible manner?
notes.back: The minor version.
notes.explanation: The minor version must also be incremented when any public functionality is marked as deprecated.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Minor version Y (x.Y.z | x > 0) MUST be incremented if new, backward compatible functionality is introduced to the public API. It MUST be incremented if any public API functionality is marked as deprecated.

notes.front: Under SemVer, which part of the version do you increment when you make incompatible changes to the public interface?
notes.back: The major version.
notes.explanation: Minor and patch are reset to 0 when the major version goes up.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Major version X (X.y.z | X > 0) MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced to the public API. It MAY also include minor and patch level changes. Patch and minor versions MUST be reset to 0 when major version is incremented.

notes.front: Version 2.4.1 of a library is current. The next release changes nothing else but marks one public method as deprecated. What should the new version be under SemVer?
notes.choices:
A) 2.4.2
B) 3.0.0
C) 2.4.1 again, with new contents
D) 2.5.0
notes.choicesExplained: A is for bug fixes only. B is for backward incompatible changes; deprecating is not removing. C breaks the rule that a released version’s contents must not change.
notes.explanation: The minor version must be incremented when public functionality is marked as deprecated, and patch resets to 0.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: It MUST be incremented if any public API functionality is marked as deprecated.

notes.front: Version 3.2.7 is current. The next release removes a public method that callers use. What should the new version be under SemVer?
notes.choicesExplained: B is for backward compatible additions. A is for bug fixes. D forgets to reset minor and patch to 0.
notes.explanation: Removing a method callers use is a backward incompatible change, so the major version goes up and the others reset.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Major version X (X.y.z | X > 0) MUST be incremented if any backward incompatible changes are introduced to the public API. It MAY also include minor and patch level changes. Patch and minor versions MUST be reset to 0 when major version is incremented.

notes.front: A tool at version 0.9.3 now runs in production at several companies whose builds depend on its interface. What do the SemVer frequently asked questions suggest?
notes.choices:
A) Stay on 0.y.z until the code is finished
B) Switch to a date-based version
C) It should probably already be 1.0.0
D) Release 0.10.0 to signal stability
notes.back: C) It should probably already be 1.0.0
notes.choicesExplained: A ignores that users now depend on it. B changes scheme without addressing stability. D stays in the “anything may change” range.
notes.explanation: The answers say software used in production should probably already be 1.0.0.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “How do I know when to release 1.0.0?”
notes.evidence: If your software is being used in production, it should probably already be 1.0.0. If you have a stable API on which users have come to depend, you should be 1.0.0.

notes.front: How is a SemVer pre-release version written, and how does it rank against the normal version?
notes.back: A hyphen and dot-separated identifiers after the patch, as in `1.0.0-alpha.1`; it has lower precedence than `1.0.0`.
notes.explanation: A pre-release is unstable and might not meet the compatibility its normal version promises.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Pre-release versions have a lower precedence than the associated normal version. A pre-release version indicates that the version is unstable and might not satisfy the intended compatibility requirements as denoted by its associated normal version. Examples: 1.0.0-alpha, 1.0.0-alpha.1

notes.front: In SemVer, what do versions that differ only in build metadata (after a `+`) have in common?
notes.back: The same precedence: build metadata is ignored when ordering versions.
notes.explanation: Build metadata plays no part in deciding which of two versions is higher.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: Build metadata MUST be ignored when determining version precedence. Thus two versions that differ only in the build metadata, have the same precedence.

notes.front: A feed holds `2.0.0-rc.1`, `2.0.0-beta.2` and `2.0.0`. Under SemVer precedence, which is the highest?
notes.choices:
A) `2.0.0`
B) `2.0.0-beta.2`
C) They are equal
D) `2.0.0-rc.1`
notes.choicesExplained: D and B are pre-releases, which rank below the normal version. C is wrong: pre-release identifiers do count in precedence (only build metadata does not).
notes.explanation: When major, minor and patch are equal, a pre-release version has lower precedence than the normal version.
notes.source: Tom Preston-Werner, “Semantic Versioning 2.0.0”, “Semantic Versioning Specification (SemVer)”
notes.evidence: When major, minor, and patch are equal, a pre-release version has lower precedence than a normal version: Example: 1.0.0-alpha < 1.0.0.

notes.front: In CalVer terminology, what do `YYYY` and `0M` stand for?
notes.back: `YYYY` is the full year (such as 2026); `0M` is the zero-padded month (01 to 12).
notes.explanation: CalVer names the date segments so each project can design the scheme that fits it.
notes.source: calver.org, “Calendar Versioning”, “Scheme”
notes.evidence: YYYY - Full year - 2006, 2016, 2106 - YY - Short year - 6, 16, 106 - 0Y - Zero-padded year - 06, 16, 106 - MM - Short month - 1, 2 ... 11, 12 - 0M - Zero-padded month - 01, 02 ... 11, 12

notes.front: Ubuntu’s first general release, in October 2004, was 4.10. Which CalVer scheme does that follow?
notes.choices:
A) `YY.0M`: short year and zero-padded month
B) `YYYY.MM`: full year and short month
C) `0M.YY`: month first
D) SemVer major.minor
notes.back: A) `YY.0M`: short year and zero-padded month
notes.choicesExplained: B would give 2004.10. C would put the month first (10.04). D would say nothing about the date.
notes.explanation: Ubuntu uses a short year and a zero-padded month, so October 2004 became 4.10.
notes.source: calver.org, “Calendar Versioning”, “Ubuntu”
notes.evidence: uses a three-segment CalVer scheme, with a short year and zero-padded month. It has done so from the very start, in October 2004, making 4.10 the first general release of Ubuntu.

notes.front: A project ships updates to a bundle of security certificates whenever outside events require it, and users care most about how recent a release is. Which versioning scheme does calver.org’s guidance point to?
notes.choices:
A) SemVer, because every update is a patch
B) A single build counter
C) CalVer, because the project is time-sensitive
D) Four-number versions
notes.back: C) CalVer, because the project is time-sensitive
notes.choicesExplained: A does not tell users how recent a release is. B carries no meaning. D is a pattern the CalVer page says convention discourages.
notes.explanation: The CalVer guidance asks whether the project is time-sensitive or driven by external changes; a yes makes CalVer a strong choice.
notes.source: calver.org, “Calendar Versioning”, “When to use CalVer”
notes.evidence: Is your project time-sensitive in any way? Do other external changes drive new project releases? - Business requirements, such as Ubuntu's focus on support schedules. - Security updates, such as certifi's need to update certificates.

notes.front: What does a SemVer number tell a consumer that a pure CalVer number does not?
notes.back: Whether the change is compatible: a bug fix, a compatible addition or a breaking change.
notes.explanation: SemVer’s increments convey the nature and risk of the change; CalVer’s segments convey when it was released.
notes.source: Microsoft, “What are feed views?”, “Nature and risk of the change” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Most teams use Semantic Versioning (SemVer) to convey this information. SemVer is widely adopted and effective for signaling nature and risk.

notes.front: In a `YAML` pipeline, what is the `publish` step keyword a shortcut for?
notes.back: The Publish Pipeline Artifact task (`PublishPipelineArtifact@1`).
notes.explanation: Both forms take the path to publish and the artifact’s name.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Publish artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The `publish` keyword is a shortcut for the Publish Pipeline Artifact task .

notes.front: In which kind of Azure Pipelines pipeline is publishing pipeline artifacts not supported?
notes.back: Release pipelines.
notes.explanation: You publish pipeline artifacts with `YAML`, the classic editor or the Azure command line, but not from a release pipeline.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Publish artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Publishing pipeline artifacts is not supported in release pipelines.

notes.front: A Linux job publishes an artifact containing a file named `report*final.txt`. A Windows job then fails to download it. Why?
notes.choices:
A) Pipeline artifacts cannot cross operating systems
B) File paths must be valid for the target environment, and a name containing `*` fails on Windows
C) The artifact had no name
D) Artifacts expire when the publishing job ends
notes.back: B) File paths must be valid for the target environment, and a name containing `*` fails on Windows
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: a job on a different operating system can consume the artifact if paths are valid. C is allowed: the name is optional. D is wrong: artifacts are removed when the run is deleted.
notes.explanation: The consuming job runs on another operating system, and that system’s file-name rules apply when it downloads.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Publish artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If you plan to consume the artifact from a job running on a different OS, you must ensure all the file paths are valid for the target environment. For example, a file name containing the character `\` or `*` will fail to download on Windows.

notes.front: A job must download the `WebApp` artifact into `$(Build.SourcesDirectory)/bin`. Which step does that?
notes.choices:
A) `download: current` with `artifact: WebApp`
B) `task: DownloadPipelineArtifact@2` with `artifact: WebApp` and `path: $(Build.SourcesDirectory)/bin`
C) `publish: $(Build.SourcesDirectory)/bin`
D) `download: current` with `target: $(Build.SourcesDirectory)/bin`
notes.back: B) `task: DownloadPipelineArtifact@2` with `artifact: WebApp` and `path: $(Build.SourcesDirectory)/bin`
notes.choicesExplained: A always uses the default location under `$(Pipeline.Workspace)`. C publishes rather than downloads. D misuses `target`, which picks the step’s execution context, not the destination.
notes.explanation: Only the task’s `path` input sets a custom download destination.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Download location” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The `target` property in the steps.download YAML schema reference is unrelated to the download destination. `target` selects the execution context that the step itself runs in

notes.front: How do pipeline artifacts relate to build artifacts in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: Pipeline artifacts are the next generation of build artifacts and the recommended way to work with artifacts.
notes.explanation: Artifacts from the Publish Build Artifacts task can still be downloaded, but the Download Pipeline Artifact task is recommended.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Migrate from build artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Pipeline artifacts are the next generation of build artifacts and are the recommended way to work with artifacts. Artifacts published using the Publish Build Artifacts task can still be downloaded using Download Build Artifacts, but we recommend using the latest Download Pipeline Artifact task instead.

notes.front: While moving from Download Build Artifacts to Download Pipeline Artifact, you keep the pattern `drop/**/*.dll` and also set `artifact: drop`. Nothing downloads. What should change?
notes.choices:
A) Add the artifact name twice
B) Remove the artifact name from the pattern, using `**/*.dll`
C) Switch back to build artifacts
D) Move the files to a feed
notes.back: B) Remove the artifact name from the pattern, using `**/*.dll`
notes.choicesExplained: A makes the mismatch worse. C avoids the recommended task instead of fixing the pattern. D confuses a package feed with pipeline artifacts.
notes.explanation: Download Pipeline Artifact patterns should not include the artifact name when a name is already given.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Migrate from build artifacts” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In the **Download Pipeline Artifact** task, patterns should not include the artifact name when an artifact name has already been specified.

notes.front: How do you use one artifact across different stages of an Azure Pipelines pipeline?
notes.back: Publish it in one stage, then download it in the next stage, using stage dependencies.
notes.explanation: The documented example copies a scripts folder in a build stage, then downloads and runs it in a second stage.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Use Artifacts across stages” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: you can now publish your artifact in one stage and then download it in the next stage leveraging dependencies.

notes.front: If there is no `.artifactignore` file, what does Azure Artifacts leave out automatically, and how do you stop that?
notes.back: The `.git` folder; create an empty `.artifactignore` file to bypass it.
notes.explanation: The automatic exclusion applies only while no `.artifactignore` exists.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Publish and download pipeline artifacts”, “Use .artifactignore” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: Azure Artifacts automatically ignore the `.git` folder path when you don't have a `.artifactignore` file. You can bypass this by creating an empty *.artifactignore* file.

notes.front: What is the default run number format in Azure Pipelines?
notes.back: `$(Date:yyyyMMdd).$(Rev:r)`
notes.explanation: That gives names such as `20260926.1`, `20260926.2` for runs on the same day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run number” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: The default value for an Azure Pipelines run number is `$(Date:yyyyMMdd).$(Rev:r)`.

notes.front: Where do you set a custom run number format in a `YAML` pipeline, and where is it not supported?
notes.back: With the `name` property at pipeline level; it is not supported in templates or stages.
notes.explanation: In Classic pipelines the same setting is Build number format under Options.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Build number configuration” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: In YAML pipelines, you can customize the run number format by using the `name` property at the pipeline level of the YAML file. The `name` property isn't supported in templates or stages.

notes.front: When does `$(Rev:r)` reset to 1?
notes.back: When any other part of the build number changes, such as the date or the version prefix.
notes.explanation: If nothing else changes, it increases by one with each completed build.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run number” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: When a build completes, if nothing else in the build number changes, the `Rev` integer value increases by one. `$(Rev:r)` resets to `1` when any other part of the build number changes.

notes.front: A pipeline uses `name: 1.0.$(Rev:r)` and its last run was 1.0.3. You change the line to `name: 1.1.$(Rev:r)`. What is the next run number?
notes.choicesExplained: A carries the old counter on. D ignores the new format. C is wrong: `$(Rev:r)` starts again at 1, not 0.
notes.explanation: Changing the version part of the format resets `$(Rev:r)` to 1.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run number” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: If your build format is `1.0.$(Rev:r)` and your last build number was **1.0.3**, if you change the version to `1.1.$(Rev:r)`, the next build number is **1.1.1**.

notes.front: A team uses `$(Rev:rr)` in its version so builds read 2.0.01, 2.0.02. Its NuGet packages then show 2.0.1 and no longer match the build number. Why?
notes.choices:
A) `$(Rev:rr)` is not a valid token
B) Some tools, including NuGet, remove leading zeros
C) Run numbers cannot contain full stops
D) The date token is missing
notes.back: B) Some tools, including NuGet, remove leading zeros
notes.choicesExplained: A is wrong: extra `r` characters are how you zero-pad `Rev`. C is wrong: the default format itself contains a full stop. D is irrelevant to padding.
notes.explanation: A zero-padded `Rev` in a version scheme causes a mismatch with artifacts whose tools strip the zeros.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run number tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: However, if you use a zero-padded `Rev` as part of a version numbering scheme, some pipeline tasks or popular tools like NuGet packages remove the leading zeros. This behavior causes a version number mismatch in the artifacts that the build produces.

notes.front: What is `$(Build.BuildId)`?
notes.back: An internal, immutable identifier, also called the Run ID, unique in the Azure DevOps organisation.
notes.explanation: Unlike `$(Rev:r)`, it does not restart each day.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Run and build numbers”, “Run number tokens” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: | `$(Build.BuildId)` | 752 | An internal, immutable ID, also called the `Run ID`, that's unique in the Azure DevOps organization.|

notes.front: How do you add a build tag automatically from a step in a `YAML` pipeline?
notes.back: With the `addbuildtag` logging command, for example `echo "##vso[build.addbuildtag]mytag"`.
notes.explanation: The command can include variables, such as the current date.
notes.source: Microsoft, “Add, remove, and use build tags”, “Add a build tag to a future build” (MicrosoftDocs/azure-devops-docs on GitHub)
notes.evidence: To automatically add a build tag to a future build in a YAML pipeline, use the `addbuildtag` logging command.

notes.front: Which two actions does GitHub provide to upload and download workflow artifacts?
notes.back: `upload-artifact` and `download-artifact`.
notes.explanation: Steps use them to store a job’s files and fetch them in another job.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Workflow artifacts”, “About workflow artifacts”
notes.evidence: provides two actions that you can use to upload and download build artifacts,

notes.front: A workflow’s build job produces a compiled binary that the deploy job in the same run needs. Should it pass the binary as an artifact or through the dependency cache?
notes.choices:
A) An artifact, because it passes files a job produced to another job in the workflow
B) Either: they are interchangeable
C) Neither: jobs cannot share files
D) The cache, because the binary changes every run
notes.back: A) An artifact, because it passes files a job produced to another job in the workflow
notes.choicesExplained: D inverts the rule: caching suits files that rarely change, such as downloaded dependencies. B is wrong: the two cannot be used interchangeably. C is wrong: artifacts exist to share files between jobs.
notes.explanation: Artifacts are for files a job produced that another job, or someone after the run, needs.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “Artifacts versus dependency caching” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/comparing-artifacts-caching.md)
notes.evidence: Use artifacts when you want to save files produced by a job to use or view after a workflow run has ended, such as built binaries or build logs, or when you want to pass files between jobs in a workflow.

notes.front: What are two pieces of information that an artifact attestation records about a build?
notes.back: Any two of: a link to the workflow; the repository, organisation, environment, commit or triggering event.
notes.explanation: Together these establish the build’s provenance.
notes.source: GitHub Docs, “About artifact attestations” (github/docs on GitHub, data/reusables/actions/about-artifact-attestations.md)
notes.evidence: * A link to the workflow associated with the artifact * The repository, organization, environment, commit SHA, and triggering event for the artifact
